content.text:
## What SPF is

When a mail server receives a message claiming to come from `@cyccommunitysailing.org`, it looks up the domain's SPF record. That's a DNS TXT record starting with `v=spf1` that lists which servers may send mail for the domain. Yours is meant to say "Google Workspace and Amazon SES."

## What's wrong

The SPF standard (RFC 7208) says a domain must publish exactly one SPF record. Yours publishes two:

```
"v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
"v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all"
```

When a receiver finds two, it doesn't pick one; the check ends in an error (a "permerror"). So every message from the domain, including Workspace mail staff send every day, arrives with no SPF protection.

There's no DKIM fallback either. Google falls back to signing Workspace mail with a Google-owned domain when you haven't set up your own DKIM key, and a receiver checking DMARC won't count that signature as vouching for `cyccommunitysailing.org`. Your DMARC policy (`p=none`) means receivers aren't told to reject that mail, so it still gets delivered. But Gmail and Yahoo now treat mail that passes neither SPF nor DKIM as suspicious, and they're stricter with automated mail. Login codes sent from `noreply@` would likely go to spam.

## A second problem I found while looking

The domain's inbound mail records include one that shouldn't be there:

```
 1 aspmx.l.google.com.         ← Google (correct)
 ...
15 feedback-smtp.us-east-2.amazonses.com.   ← SES
```

Together with the SES SPF record, this looks like Amazon SES's "custom MAIL FROM" setup. SES has you publish that pair on a subdomain, such as `mail.cyccommunitysailing.org`, so bounced SES mail goes back to Amazon. Here both records sit on the root domain, most likely because the host field was left blank at Porkbun when they were added. I checked the common subdomain names and found nothing there. The SES MX record is only a backup behind Google's, so it rarely gets used. But if Google's servers were ever unreachable, mail meant for your inboxes could go to Amazon instead, and it would bounce.

## The fix

Either way, get down to one SPF record on the root domain. What else to change depends on whether SES is sending mail today:

- **If SES isn't in use:** delete the SES SPF record and the SES MX record, leaving `v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all`. That's the cleanest result.
- **If SES is in use with a custom MAIL FROM:** move both SES records to the MAIL FROM subdomain configured in SES, and keep only Google's record on the root domain.
- **If you're not sure:** merge them into `v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:amazonses.com ~all` and remove the root SES MX record. That's safe either way, and you can clean up once you know.

DKIM is needed in every case. The stray `v=DMARC1; p=none;` record at the domain root is harmless, but it duplicates the real one at `_dmarc` and can go.

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='.claude/plans/community-roster.md'
s=open(p).read()
old="""3. Delete the stray `v=DMARC1` TXT record at the apex. `_dmarc` already holds the real one."""
new=old+"""
4. Delete the SES `feedback-smtp` MX record at the apex. It belongs on an SES custom MAIL FROM
   subdomain, and at the apex it can take inbound mail if Google's MX hosts are unreachable. Once
   it is known whether SES sends for the domain, drop `include:amazonses.com` or move it to that
   subdomain."""
assert old in s
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old,new))
EOF
